newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: INTERVIEW-Golden Vale sees improvement in 97.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Golden Vale sees improvement in 97.

text.p: Irish food company Golden Vale Plc said on Tuesday that it hoped to savour a better outturn in 1997 after reporting a sharp drop in 1996 profits, mainly due to a downturn in the industry.

"So far so good," newly appointed group managing director Jim Murphy told Reuters. "The first few months of 1997 are looking quite good we are certainly getting comfort around meeting the general profit expectations that are out in the market place for Golden Vale," he said.
Golden Vale earlier announced a drop in 1996 pre-tax profit to 6.3 million Irish pounds ($9.8 million) from 16.5 million on turnover of 561 million down from 564 million in 1995.
Murphy, who took on the mantle of group managing director two months ago, said the food group was expecting an improved performance across its divisions in 1997.

"We are looking at an improved performance in our cheese business and we have already taken action to resolve the issues in Holland," Murphy said. "Generally the business is performing better and other products business such as St Brendan's creme liqueurs and our spreads business continue to do well."

Golden Vale's Dutch operation saw a sharp drop from a 0.5 million Irish pounds contribution in 1995 to a negative contribution of 1.0 million punts in 1996 which the group said was due to lower margins, volume loss and some one-off costs.

Murphy said the priorities for 1997 were to restore stability, improve profitability and to shape the future direction of the troubled group. He said all areas were under review and he would not rule out further cost cutting if necessary.

Golden Vale said the drop of 9.2 million Irish pounds in operating profit before exceptional items to 12.1 million was entirely due to the imbalance between milk price and weak market prices for butter and milk powders.
It said selling prices in 1996 had fallen by nine percent for bulk butter and seven percent for skim milk powder compared with a fall in milk price of one percent.
Murphy said that despite the disappointing profit performance it had reduced its borrowings by 9.3 million Irish pounds in the year, reducing gearing from 78 to 60 percent.
The group said this margin pressure had been partially alleviated by higher sales volumes, improvement in retail butter margins and the continued development of its added value powder business.

"Any improvement in performance in this business sector is clearly heavily dependent on absolute levels of milk price but is also dependent upon continuing the drive to add value to the basic products and to reduce the cost base of the business," he said.

Golden Vale said turnover in its cheese division had fallen by 2.4 percent to 123 million Irish pounds, operating profit was down 0.3 million punts to 0.8 million while the margin on sales had dropped 0.2 percent to 0.7 percent.
The launch costs of "Cheesestrings" in the British and Irish markets had totalled 2.5 million Irish pounds in 1996, the benefit from which would not come through in volume sales until 1997, he said.

"In terms of cheese, our branded Cheesestrings will be on stream for the full year in 1997 which means we will have the benefit of a full year's volume so there will be quite a turnaround there," Murphy said.
